```python
from gurobipy import *

def solve_problem():
    m = Model("MultiObjective_Transportation")
    m.setParam('TimeLimit', 300)

    # --- Data ---
    I = 7  # sources
    J = 5  # destinations
    K = 3  # max suppliers per store
    w_cost = 0.6
    w_emission = 0.4

    supplies = [110, 152, 210, 107, 144, 104, 162]
    demands = [21, 17, 44, 12, 27]
    cost_matrix = [[8.49, 28.46, 22.6, 19.24, 6.62], [19.23, 6.1, 17.28, 25.04, 23.47], [3.19, 14.17, 16.18, 10.3, 7.86], [24.01, 17.81, 22.43, 18.0, 19.72], [8.74, 28.6, 27.92, 10.48, 19.47], [13.7, 10.39, 14.71, 4.32, 26.58], [4.39, 12.42, 19.01, 13.93, 16.56]]
    emission_matrix = [[15.09, 1.0, 11.59, 10.61, 16.83], [11.0, 13.25, 6.0, 8.2, 4.37], [20.0, 6.89, 6.84, 4.92, 16.61], [16.58, 4.71, 2.29, 3.34, 2.91], [16.21, 4.81, 9.84, 3.87, 7.63], [15.77, 10.08, 12.19, 7.84, 11.24], [9.32, 12.79, 14.61, 15.88, 10.76]]
    fixed_costs = [[89, 229, 72, 300, 281], [264, 54, 106, 63, 164], [300, 84, 157, 234, 189], [121, 216, 159, 225, 238], [188, 193, 58, 160, 278], [223, 255, 184, 188, 234], [209, 230, 211, 174, 122]]
    moq = [[12, 5, 15, 14, 7], [17, 17, 5, 8, 12], [10, 5, 7, 5, 12], [5, 10, 6, 17, 15], [13, 11, 17, 12, 10], [13, 16, 17, 18, 14], [6, 5, 17, 6, 10]]

    # Big-M per route
    total_demand = sum(demands)
    big_M = [[min(supplies[i], total_demand) for j in range(J)] for i in range(I)]

    # --- Variables ---
    # Continuous: shipment quantities
    x = {}
    for i in range(I):
        for j in range(J):
            x[(i,j)] = m.addVar(lb=0, vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, name=f"Ship_S{i}_D{j}")

    # Binary: route-open indicators
    y = {}
    for i in range(I):
        for j in range(J):
            y[(i,j)] = m.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY, name=f"RouteOpen_S{i}_D{j}")

    # --- Objective ---
    # Weighted variable cost + fixed setup costs
    m.setObjective(
        quicksum(
            (w_cost * cost_matrix[i][j] + w_emission * emission_matrix[i][j]) * x[(i,j)]
            for i in range(I) for j in range(J)
        )
        + quicksum(fixed_costs[i][j] * y[(i,j)] for i in range(I) for j in range(J)),
        GRB.MINIMIZE
    )

    # --- Constraints ---
    # C1: Supply
    for i in range(I):
        m.addConstr(
            quicksum(x[(i,j)] for j in range(J)) <= supplies[i],
            name=f"Supply_S{i}")

    # C2: Demand
    for j in range(J):
        m.addConstr(
            quicksum(x[(i,j)] for i in range(I)) >= demands[j],
            name=f"Demand_D{j}")

    # C3: Linking — can only ship if route is open
    for i in range(I):
        for j in range(J):
            m.addConstr(
                x[(i,j)] <= big_M[i][j] * y[(i,j)],
                name=f"Link_S{i}_D{j}")

    # C4: Minimum order quantity
    for i in range(I):
        for j in range(J):
            m.addConstr(
                x[(i,j)] >= moq[i][j] * y[(i,j)],
                name=f"MOQ_S{i}_D{j}")

    # C5: Max suppliers per store
    for j in range(J):
        m.addConstr(
            quicksum(y[(i,j)] for i in range(I)) <= K,
            name=f"MaxSupplier_D{j}")

    m.optimize()
    return m
```

Subject: Balancing Shipping Cost and Carbon Impact Under Real-World Operating Rules
Date: Today
From: Sustainability & Logistics Director
To: Supply Chain Leadership

Context
We are refining our transportation plan to meet store service commitments while balancing financial performance and environmental impact. Each warehouse-to-store lane carries both a monetary shipping cost per unit and a carbon emission rate per unit. In practice, the lowest-cost lanes tend to have higher emissions, creating a clear trade-off. We must navigate this tension transparently and consistently with management’s priorities.

Operational rules we must honor
- Route activation costs: Opening a lane requires a fixed setup expense covering contracting, compliance, and dock readiness. A lane is either active or inactive; once active, the setup cost is incurred regardless of the volume eventually shipped.
- Minimum order quantities: To avoid inefficient handling and partial loads, any active lane must carry at least a defined minimum shipment quantity. If we cannot justify that minimum, the lane should remain inactive.
- Supplier limits per store: To control receiving complexity and maintain service discipline, each store may source from no more than a set number of warehouses. This cap necessitates thoughtful consolidation and may push some volume to slightly higher-cost or lower-emission alternatives to keep within the limit.

Supply and demand guardrails
- Warehouse supplies: Each warehouse has a finite inventory or outbound capacity. Shipments from any warehouse cannot exceed its available supply.
- Store demand: Each store has a required minimum demand that must be met. Shortfalls are not acceptable; any plan must allocate sufficient inbound volume to every store.

Management priorities and how we will score options
Leadership has set relative importance for cost and emissions. We will evaluate candidate plans using a composite score that:
- Applies the cost importance to total variable transportation cost,
- Applies the emissions importance to total carbon emissions, and
- Adds all route activation/setup costs at full value (these are not weighted).
This scoring approach reflects our commitment to both affordability and sustainability while recognizing that standing up a lane imposes a real cash outlay independent of volume.

Business goal and decision required
We aim to determine which lanes to activate and how much to ship on each lane so that:
- Warehouse inventory is not exceeded and store demand is met,
- Every activated lane moves at least its required minimum quantity,
- Each store receives from no more than the allowed number of warehouses, and
- The combined cost-and-emissions score (with setup costs added in full) is as low as possible under the above rules.
Deliverables will include the list of activated lanes, shipment quantities by lane, and an assessment of how the plan performs on cost and carbon relative to management’s stated priorities. We will also flag any pinch points where operational rules materially drive trade-offs, to guide discussion on potential policy or supplier adjustments.
